Loss Prevention Managers
11-9199.08
Bright Outlook Updated 2025

Plan and direct policies, procedures, or systems to prevent the loss of assets. Determine risk exposure or potential liability, and develop risk control measures.

Sample of reported job titles: Asset Protection Manager, Logistics Loss Prevention Manager, Loss Control Manager, Loss Prevention Director, Loss Prevention Manager, Loss Prevention Operations Director, Loss Prevention Operations Manager, Loss Prevention Supervisor, Market Asset Protection Manager

Occupation-Specific Information

Tasks

  • Coordinate or conduct internal investigations of problems such as employee theft and violations of corporate loss prevention policies.
    Related occupations
  • Administer systems and programs to reduce loss, maintain inventory control, or increase safety.
    Related occupations
  • Review loss prevention exception reports and cash discrepancies to ensure adherence to guidelines.
    Related occupations
  • Train loss prevention staff, retail managers, or store employees on loss control and prevention measures.
    Related occupations
  • Investigate or interview individuals suspected of shoplifting or internal theft.
    Related occupations
  • Provide recommendations and solutions in crisis situations such as workplace violence, protests, and demonstrations.
    Related occupations
  • Identify potential for loss and develop strategies to eliminate it.
    Related occupations
  • Hire or supervise loss prevention staff.
    Related occupations
  • Advise retail managers on compliance with applicable codes, laws, regulations, or standards.
    Related occupations
  • Develop and maintain partnerships with federal, state, or local law enforcement agencies or members of the retail loss prevention community.
    Related occupations
  • Perform or direct inventory investigations in response to shrink results outside of acceptable ranges.
    Related occupations
  • Maintain documentation of all loss prevention activity.
    Related occupations
  • Assess security needs across locations to ensure proper deployment of loss prevention resources, such as staff and technology.
    Related occupations
  • Monitor compliance to operational, safety, or inventory control procedures, including physical security standards.
    Related occupations
  • Verify correct use and maintenance of physical security systems, such as closed-circuit television, merchandise tags, and burglar alarms.
    Related occupations
  • Visit stores to ensure compliance with company policies and procedures.
    Related occupations
  • Analyze retail data to identify current or emerging trends in theft or fraud.
    Related occupations
  • Direct loss prevention audit programs including target store audits, maintenance audits, safety audits, or electronic article surveillance (EAS) audits.
    Related occupations
  • Collaborate with law enforcement to investigate and solve external theft or fraud cases.
    Related occupations
  • Coordinate theft and fraud investigations involving career criminals or organized group activities.
    Related occupations
  • Supervise surveillance, detection, or criminal processing related to theft and criminal cases.
    Related occupations
  • Perform cash audits and deposit investigations to fully account for store cash.
    Related occupations
  • Recommend improvements in loss prevention programs, staffing, scheduling, or training.
    Related occupations
  • Direct installation of covert surveillance equipment, such as security cameras.
    Related occupations
  • Monitor and review paperwork procedures and systems to prevent error-related shortages.
    Related occupations
  • Advise retail establishments on development of loss-investigation procedures.
    Related occupations
  • Maintain databases such as bad check logs, reports on multiple offenders, and alarm activation lists.
    Related occupations

Experience Requirements

Job Zone

Title
Job Zone Four: Considerable Preparation Needed
Education
Most of these occupations require a four-year bachelor's degree, but some do not.
Related Experience
A considerable amount of work-related skill, knowledge, or experience is needed for these occupations. For example, an accountant must complete four years of college and work for several years in accounting to be considered qualified.
Job Training
Employees in these occupations usually need several years of work-related experience, on-the-job training, and/or vocational training.
Job Zone Examples
Many of these occupations involve coordinating, supervising, managing, or training others. Examples include real estate brokers, sales managers, database administrators, graphic designers, conservation scientists, art directors, and cost estimators.
SVP Range
(7.0 to < 8.0)
